options: Repeatedly reads a device status bit to see if service is needed
Stops the clock until the disk finishes
Lets the device write the register file with no setup
Always services the keyboard before the disk
questions.explanation: The CPU asks “are you ready?” in a loop. An interrupt lets the device signal instead, so the CPU can do other work.

options: Addresses of handlers, selected by an interrupt number
The user’s open files
Cache tags
The ready queue
questions.explanation: The hardware uses the interrupt number as an index and jumps to the address it finds. The handler itself lives elsewhere.

options: A device can move a block while the CPU does other work, instead of the CPU copying every byte
The CPU no longer needs a clock
Interrupts become illegal for the rest of the boot
Virtual memory is turned off
questions.explanation: The CPU programs the DMA engine and is told when the block is finished. It does not sit in a load/store loop for every byte.
traps: DMA does not power the CPU down, and it usually ends with an interrupt.

questions.prompt: Two unmasked interrupts are pending. The CPU should service
options: The one with the more urgent priority
Whichever belongs to the older program
Always the keyboard, regardless of priority
Neither, until the current process exits
questions.explanation: Priority is how the machine decides which pending request is first. A mask can also take a device out of the contest.

questions.prompt: Before a handler runs, something must preserve enough state to resume the interrupted program. Which items are part of that idea?
options: The return address (program counter)
The condition flags
The inode of every file on disk
Registers the handler would otherwise overwrite
questions.explanation: The interrupted program needs its PC, flags, and any registers the handler uses. Saving every file is not part of taking an interrupt.

options: Device registers appear at addresses the CPU can load and store
Every file is cached in RAM
Interrupts are stored as pages
The disk is the only memory in the machine
questions.explanation: A load or store to a special address talks to a device. There is no separate I/O opcode required for that device.

questions.prompt: A non-maskable interrupt differs from a maskable one because
options: The ordinary interrupt mask cannot quietly ignore it
It has no handler
It is never allowed to preempt anything
It is only the keyboard repeat
questions.explanation: Maskable interrupts respect an enable flag. A non-maskable interrupt is reserved for events the machine must notice, such as a serious hardware fault.

questions.prompt: A page fault raised by the running instruction is best classed as
options: An exception from the instruction stream, not a device interrupt
A disk DMA completion
A clock tick
A context switch by definition
questions.explanation: Device interrupts arrive from outside. Exceptions are caused by the instruction being executed. The OS may do I/O to fix a page fault, but the original event is an exception.
traps: Calling every control transfer a device interrupt.

questions.prompt: Why does a handler often mask interrupts of the same priority at the very start?
questions.answer: So it can save state and touch device data without being re-entered in the middle of that prologue.
questions.explanation: Once the handler is in a safe state it may re-enable selected interrupts. The mask is about the dangerous first moments, not about never sharing the CPU.
